title: Knowledge check: The Server Object

questions.prompt: Which subtopic is explicitly listed under “The Server Object” in the attached Classic ASP curriculum?
questions.explanation: The PDF lists “Introduction to Server” under lesson 44, “The Server Object”. The distractors belong to other lesson topics.

questions.prompt: When applying “The Server Object” in a legacy Classic ASP application, which approach is strongest?
options: Validate input, bind values as ADO parameters, and close database resources reliably.
Concatenate user values directly into SQL.
Return the full connection string to the browser when debugging.
Keep every Recordset open for the whole session.
questions.answer_key: Validate input, bind values as ADO parameters, and close database resources reliably.
questions.explanation: This approach keeps the server object testable and respects Classic ASP/IIS runtime boundaries. The exact IIS, provider, or component behavior must be checked in the target test environment.

questions.prompt: Before marking work on “The Server Object” ready for review, what evidence should be recorded?
options: Claim the production deployment passed without running it.
Delete diagnostic evidence before recording the outcome.
Treat a successful happy-path test as proof of all security properties.
Document the observed result, tool/runtime version, and one meaningful failure or edge case.
questions.answer_key: Document the observed result, tool/runtime version, and one meaningful failure or edge case.
questions.explanation: Good maintenance evidence includes the expected and observed result, relevant version/runtime assumptions, and a boundary or failure test. Never claim an execution/deployment test that was not run.
